Source slide page 3 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Conducting polymers

Polymers are generally insulators because the organic molecules of which they are composed have no free electrons to carry current

An organic polymer with highly delocalized pi-electron system, having electrical conductance of the order of an electrical conductor is called a conducting polymer

Also known as synthetic metals

Source slide page 4 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Development :

1977 - Heeger, Macdiarmid & Shirakawa demonstrated conductivity of polyacetylene can be increased 13 times by doping with electron acceptors and donors

Norman et. al - achieved conductance of polyacetylene equal to copper

Doping with less than 10% of chemical species results in dramatic changes in electrical, electronic, magnetic and optical properties of polymers – hence it is a new class of polymers

2000 - Heeger, Macdiarmid & Shirakawa won the Nobel prize for Chemistry

Source slide page 5 (extracted text):

Source:https://www.researchgate.net/figure/3Molecular-structure-of-some-typical-conducting-polymers_fig2_304023062

Source slide page 6 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Conducting polymers conduct electricity due to delocalization of π electrons 
An organic polymer can be converted into conducting polymer if it has :
• linear structure
• extensive conjugation in its polymeric back bone

POLYACETYLENE

POLYPHENYLENE

Source:https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Some-Examples-for-Conducting-Polymers_fig4_269993677

Source slide page 7 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

These materials in pure form are not conductors but on doping (Introduction of charged chemical species) conduction increases

Types of Doping

Oxidative doping

Reductive doping

Proton doping

Source slide page 8 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Oxidative doping (p-doping) 
In this process, pi-backbone of a polymer is partially oxidized using a suitable oxidizing agent 
This creates positively charged sites on the polymer backbone which are the current carriers for conduction 
The oxidizing agents used are Iodine in CCl4, HBF4 etc.

Source slide page 9 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Reductive doping (n-doping) :
 In this process, pi-backbone of a polymer is partially reduced using a suitable reducing agent 
This creates negatively charged sites on the polymer backbone which are the current carriers for conduction 
The reducing agent used is sodium naphthalide in THF

Source slide page 10 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Protonic acid doping :
 In this technique, current carrying charged species (+ve and –ve) are created by using a protonic acid as dopant

 Doping of polyaniline is a typical example of this type of doping 

In polyaniline, current carrying charged species (+ve and –ve) are created by protonation of imine nitrogen

[00:00:00.740] Hello everyone, welcome back to this course on engineering chemistry.
[00:00:06.052] We will continue with module seven on functional materials that is polymers and today's class we are going to talk about conducting polymers, a brief introduction, the types of dopamine, the applications of conducting polymers.
[00:00:22.916] Polymers are generally known for their insulating property because the organic molecules of which they are composed have no free electrons to carry current.
[00:00:35.332] So when conducting polymers were discovered, it was a very big revolution in the polymer industry.
[00:00:44.740] So, how would you define a conducting polymer? An organic polymer with highly delocalized pi electron system and having an electrical conductance of the order of an electrical conductor. Such a polymer was referred to as a conducting polymer. For example,
[00:01:04.516] We know that copper has very copper metal has very high conductivity of the order of 10 raised to the power of eight sements per meter, whereas Teflon has
[00:01:20.772] conductance of 10 to the power of minus 8 siemens per meter. And if you have doped polyaniline, it is found to have 10 to the power of 5 sements per meter. So if you look at doped polyaniline
[00:01:43.428] then the conductance is found to be ten to the power of five sevens per meter. Now this is very close, or rather closer to that of
[00:01:53.312] copper which is 10 to the power of 8 whereas teflon as I mentioned just now is 10 to the power of minus 8. So Teflon is used as an insulator. Now when you see duped polyaniline we understand that the conductivity is very close to that of a metal. So these
[00:02:10.960] These are also known as synthetic metals. So let us talk about the development of conducting polymers because just recently in the year 2000.
[00:02:24.224] Heger, McDermott, and Shirakawa won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for the du discovery of conducting polymers. So in nineteen seventy seven, Heger, McDermott, and Shirakawa demonstrated that the conductivity of polyacetylene can be increased
[00:02:41.872] thirteen times by doping with electron acceptors or and donors. Now normal etal achieved a conductance of polyacetylene to that of copper.
[00:02:53.412] Now it was found that doping with less than ten percent of chemical species in these polymers resulted in dramatic changes in electrical, electronic, magnetic, and optical properties of the polymers, and hence these were clapped as a new
[00:03:11.184] class of polymers known as conducting polymers. So do all polymers conduct? No. The answer is definitely no. And let us have a look at some examples of such polymers.
[00:03:28.160] Now these polymers listed here are known to conduct after doping. For example, polyacetylene, then we have polyphenylin, then this is polypyro.
[00:03:42.052] poly thiophene, polyaniline, and here we can see polyphenylin vinyline. So there is something special about all these polymers which become conducting after they are doped. So let us see what is that special feature.
[00:04:00.740] Now these conducting polymers conduct electricity due to delocalization of the pi electrons. So what would be requirement the requirement for an organic polymer to be converted into a conducting polymer?
[00:04:16.176] what we can see they have a linear structure. All those polymers which we listed just now they have a linear structure and here's I've taken just two examples. So that of polyacetylene and polyphenyline we can see that they are linear and apart from that one more important property
[00:04:33.840] Which should be there in their structure, and that is extensive conjugation in its polymer backbone. What would that mean? That they should have alternate.
[00:04:44.512] single and double bond. So then it is possible to have delocalization of the pi electron. So all these conducting polymers they are
[00:04:54.640] uh have they have these special features like a linear structure and also extensive conjugation in their polymer backbone.

[00:05:42.724] Now what is done here is
[00:05:45.440] The pi backbone of the polymer is partially oxidized with a suitable oxidizing agent. Now we know that what does an oxidizing agent do? It is going to take away electron from the polymer backbone. And now we understand why we chose a

[00:09:13.668] The third type of doping is known as protonic acid doping. Now, as the name suggests, we are going to use protonic acid as a dopant. So basically, H plus is used as a dopant here. And what is here the current carrying

[00:13:06.244] Now we know that the electrolyte can be conducting in nature, ionic conductance is found there. But when we talk of electrodes, we are talking of electronic conduction. Now what we saw in conducting polymers
[00:13:20.736] is electronic conduction because the electron could move through the polymer chain. So therefore they will be used as electrode material and because they are lightweight we expect a very high power to weight ratio.
[00:13:35.876] Then they can be used as conductive tracts on PCBs normally we see copper being printed there. So that can be replaced by these conducting polymers. Then they can be used as sensors.
[00:13:47.392] Like humidity sensor, gas sensor, radiation sensor, biosensors, etc. Then electrochromic display window, specially polyaniline, is known to have different colours in different atmospheres. So we can have a completely
